Excuse me. You are the group from Brazil, yes? I am Yelena, from Kazan.
Yes, that is us. I am Dejair. Do you work on pain as well?
I do. I investigate chronic pain after surgery. And you? What exactly do you investigate?
I investigate nerve damage caused by leprosy. The infection ends, but the pain does not stop.
Interesting. Does your group develop new drugs for that?
No, we do not develop drugs. We test treatments that already exist, and we look at the side effects.
That is our problem too. Patients stop the treatment and we do not know why. How many patients does your study involve?
About ninety, in three centres. Do you collaborate with hospitals, or only with your university?
With two hospitals. We published a paper on this in March. I can send it to you.
Please do. And I will send you ours. Do you have a card?

My name is Yelena Sokolova and I am a researcher at a medical university in Kazan. I investigate chronic pain after surgery. My group collaborates with two hospitals, and our work involves about four hundred patients every year. We do not develop new drugs. We test treatments that already exist, and we measure the side effects that patients report at home. Last year we published two papers on this, and the second one is the reason I am here. I want to know how other groups measure pain when the patient is not in the hospital.

Good afternoon. I am Arun Menon, from Kochi, in the south of India. My field is neurology and I work on nerve damage in patients with infectious disease. Our clinical trial started three years ago and it involves six centres. I do not run the trial alone. I collaborate with a statistician, two nurses and a physiotherapist, and we meet every Monday. The most difficult part is not the science. The most difficult part is that patients live far away, and many of them stop the treatment before the end. That is the problem I would like to discuss with you this week.
